facts.fact: Article 1 calls India, that is Bharat, a Union of States; territory = states, UTs and acquired territories.
Article 2 lets Parliament admit or establish new states (Sikkim).
An Art 3 bill needs the President's recommendation; the affected state's views are not binding.
Laws under Articles 2 and 3 are not Art 368 amendments (Art 4).
Berubari (1960): ceding territory needs an Art 368 amendment (9th Amendment).
The 100th Amendment (2015) implemented the India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement.
Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among states and no state can secede (UPSC 2017).
India is an indestructible union of destructible states.
The S.K. Dhar Commission (1948) rejected linguistic reorganisation.
The JVP Committee (1948) was Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
Potti Sriramulu died on 15 December 1952 after a 58-day fast for a Telugu state.
Andhra State, the first linguistic state, was formed on 1 October 1953 with Kurnool as capital.
The Fazal Ali SRC (1953) included K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru; it reported in 1955.
The States Reorganisation Act 1956 created 14 states and 6 UTs; AP was formed on 1 November 1956.
Maharashtra and Gujarat were carved out of Bombay in 1960.
Nagaland became the 16th state in 1963.
Haryana was carved out of Punjab in 1966.
Manipur, Tripura and Meghalaya became states in 1972.
Sikkim became the 22nd state in 1975 by the 36th Amendment.
Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa (25th) became states in 1987.
Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand were formed in 2000.
Telangana became the 29th state on 2 June 2014 under the AP Reorganisation Act 2014.
J&K was bifurcated into two UTs on 31 October 2019, leaving 28 states.
Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu merged on 26 January 2020, giving 8 UTs.
Federal features: two governments, division of powers, written rigid Constitution, supremacy, independent judiciary, bicameralism.
An independent judiciary is the essential federal feature (UPSC 2021).
Unitary features: strong Centre, single citizenship, Art 3, emergencies, appointed Governors, All India Services, integrated judiciary.
K.C. Wheare called India quasi-federal.
Granville Austin called it cooperative federalism; Morris-Jones bargaining federalism; Ivor Jennings a centralising federation.
Indian federation follows the Canadian model, with residuary power in the Union.
S.R. Bommai (1994) held federalism part of the basic structure.
Article 245: Parliament legislates for all or part of India, and its extra-territorial laws are valid.
The Seventh Schedule (Art 246) has Union (97→100), State (66→61) and Concurrent (47→52) lists.
Article 246A (101st Amendment 2016) lets both Parliament and states make GST laws.
Residuary power is with Parliament (Art 248).
Under Art 249 a Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds present and voting lets Parliament legislate on a State List subject for one year (UPSC 2016).
Parliament can legislate on the State List during a National Emergency (Art 250).
Under Art 252 two or more states may ask Parliament to legislate, e.g. Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972 and Water Act 1974.
Parliament can implement treaties without state consent (Art 253; UPSC 2013).
On the Concurrent List the Union law prevails unless the state law was reserved and assented by the President (Art 254).
The 42nd Amendment moved education, forests, weights and measures, wild animals and birds, and administration of justice to the Concurrent List.
Sarkaria wanted residuary taxation with Parliament and other residuary matters on the Concurrent List.
States must comply with Union laws and the Union may give directions (Art 256).
Under Art 257 the Union may direct states on communications of military importance and railways.
Article 258A (7th Amendment) lets states entrust functions to the Union.
Article 261 requires full faith and credit to public acts and judicial proceedings.
Article 312 creates All India Services on a Rajya Sabha two-thirds resolution; the Indian Forest Service came in 1966.
Under Art 365, failure to obey Union directions lets the President hold the state machinery failed.
Stamp duties (Art 268) are levied by the Union but collected and kept by states.
Article 269 taxes are levied and collected by the Union and assigned to states; Art 269A covers IGST.
Since the 80th Amendment (2000) all central taxes form a divisible pool (Art 270).
Surcharges (Art 271) are not shared with states.
Art 275 grants are statutory on FC advice; Art 282 grants are discretionary.
A state indebted to the Centre needs its consent to borrow (Art 293).
The GST Council is chaired by the Union Finance Minister, Nirmala Sitharaman.
GST Council decisions need three-fourths of weighted votes — Centre one-third, states two-thirds; quorum one-half.
GST began on 1 July 2017.
Mohit Minerals (2022): GST Council recommendations are not binding.
GST 2.0 from 22 September 2025 has 5% and 18% slabs and 40% on demerit goods.
A Finance Commission has a chairman and four members under the 1951 Miscellaneous Provisions Act.
K.C. Neogy chaired the first Finance Commission.
The 15th FC under N.K. Singh fixed the states' share at 41%.
The 16th FC under Arvind Panagariya was constituted on 31 December 2023 for 2026-31.
Andhra Pradesh's share of the divisible pool under the 16th FC is 4.22%.
During a National Emergency Parliament legislates on the State List and the Union may direct states (Art 250, 353).
During a National Emergency the President may alter revenue sharing (Art 354).
The 44th Amendment replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion" as a ground for Art 352.
National Emergency was declared in 1962, 1971 and 1975.
Under President's Rule the state legislature's powers are exercised by Parliament (UPSC 2018).
President's Rule is approved within two months by simple majority, renewed every six months, up to three years.
President's Rule beyond one year needs a National Emergency and an Election Commission certificate (44th Amendment).
Financial Emergency (Art 360) has never been declared.
Article 356 was first used in Punjab in 1951 and has been used over 100 times.
Manipur was under President's Rule from 13 February 2025 to 4 February 2026.
S.R. Bommai (1994): Art 356 is reviewable, majority is tested on the floor, and the Assembly is only suspended until Parliament approves.
The ARC (1966) study team on Centre-state relations was led by M.C. Setalvad.
The Rajamannar Committee (1969) was set up by Tamil Nadu to seek state autonomy.
The Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973) wanted the Centre limited to defence, foreign affairs, currency and communications.
The West Bengal Memorandum (1977) sought to replace "Union" by "Federal".
Sarkaria Commission (1983-88): R.S. Sarkaria with B. Sivaraman and S.R. Sen; 247 recommendations.
Sarkaria said Art 356 should be used only as a last resort and asked for a permanent Inter-State Council.
Punchhi Commission (2007-10) proposed a localised emergency for districts.
The NCRWC (2000-02) was headed by M.N. Venkatachaliah.
The Inter-State Council (Art 263) was set up in 1990 on Sarkaria's advice, chaired by the PM, with all CMs and six Union ministers.
Five Zonal Councils, statutory under the SR Act 1956, are chaired by the Union Home Minister.
AP is in the Southern Zonal Council with Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Puducherry.
The North Eastern Council (1971 Act) added Sikkim in 2002.
The Planning Commission was set up on 15 March 1950 by cabinet resolution and replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015.
The National Development Council (1952), Planning Commission and Zonal Councils are not in the Constitution (UPSC 2013).
Article 262 and the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956 bar courts from water disputes.
The River Boards Act 1956 has never been used to create a board.
KWDT-I was under R.S. Bachawat (1969); KWDT-II under Brijesh Kumar (2004).
The Godavari tribunal (1969) was also headed by R.S. Bachawat.
The Vamsadhara tribunal (2010) concerns Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
The AP Reorganisation Act 2014 created the Krishna and Godavari River Management Boards.
UTs are administered by the President through an administrator (Art 239); Part VIII, Art 239-241.
Article 239A (14th Amendment, 1962) provides Puducherry's legislature.
Article 239AA (69th Amendment, 1991) gives Delhi a 70-member Assembly; police, public order and land stay with the Centre.
Delhi has 7 Lok Sabha and 3 Rajya Sabha seats.
Article 239AB provides for President's rule in Delhi.
Under Art 240 the President makes regulations for Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep, DNH & DD.
GNCTD v. Union (May 2023) gave Delhi's elected government control of services; the GNCTD (Amendment) Act 2023 followed.
The J&K UT has an Assembly; Ladakh has none.
The Fifth Schedule (Art 244(1)) covers Scheduled Areas in ten states including Andhra Pradesh.
A Tribes Advisory Council has up to 20 members, three-fourths ST MLAs; the Governor reports yearly.
Under the Fifth Schedule the Governor may bar transfer of tribal land (UPSC 2022).
PESA 1996 extends panchayats to Fifth Schedule areas.
Samatha v. State of AP (1997) voided mining leases of tribal land to private companies (UPSC 2019).
The Sixth Schedule (Art 244(2)) covers Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
Autonomous District Councils have up to 30 members (26 elected, 4 nominated) for five years.
Both Schedules protect Scheduled Tribes (UPSC 2015).
